units.title: The Immune System
units.intro:
**Antigen** = foreign marker. **Antibody** = protein shaped to stick to that marker. White cells: some eat pathogens (phagocytes), some remember and make antibodies (lymphocytes).

**Active immunity:** your body meets the antigen (infection or vaccine) and makes its own memory. Lasts. **Passive:** you borrow ready antibodies (breast milk, injection). Fast but short.

cards.title: 4.1 Antigens and Antibodies
body: Anything that can trigger an immune response in the body is called an **antigen**.
An antigen can be a whole microbe (bacteria or a small parasite, such as a virus) or even a part of a microbe.
Tissue or cells from a donor (apart from an identical twin) can also act as antigens if given to a recipient.
In the recipient’s body, this tissue is capable of triggering an immune response, because it is foreign to the recipient.
Antibodies are protein substances produced by white blood cells in response to antigens.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Distinguish between non-specific and specific defenses**
* Non-specific (innate) defenses act as general barriers to all pathogens. These include skin, mucus, and stomach acid.
* Specific (acquired) defenses target one particular antigen and include B-lymphocytes and their tailored antibodies.

**Final Result:**
**Highly specific antibodies produced by B-lymphocytes**.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Determine natural vs. artificial and active vs. passive**
* The child contracts the pathogen naturally through exposure, so it is **natural**.
* The child's own immune system is stimulated to produce its own antibodies and memory cells, so it is **active**.

**Final Result:**
**Naturally acquired active immunity**.

body: First lines: skin, mucus, acid in stomach, tears with lysozyme — non-specific. Second: inflammation, phagocytes. Third: specific lymphocytes. Memory cells make the second meeting faster and stronger — that is why vaccines work and why measles is usually once.

Active natural = you catch the disease. Active artificial = vaccine. Passive natural = antibodies in breast milk / placenta. Passive artificial = ready antiserum. Immunosuppression and allergies are “immune system mis-firing or under-firing” stories if the book mentions them.

cards.title: 4.2.1 Active Immunity
body: Natural acquired active immunity: This type of immunity is produced when a disease-causing agent is introduced into the body by natural means (non-intentional).
For example when an individual is infected, the body produces specific antibodies against the disease-causing antigens or their products.
The antibodies continue to form after recovery, resulting in permanent active immunity.
Diphtheria, measles and mumps are diseases that often trigger this kind of immune response.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Passive Immunity
body: Natural acquired passive immunity: This is immunity that is acquired naturally when an unborn infant receives antibodies from its mother through the placenta or in the first breast-milk received from the already immune mother.
Artificial acquired passive immunity: This is an immunity that is acquired when an individual receives antibodies produced in another individual (human to human) or animal (animal to human).
The introduction of serum that contains ready-made antibodies is important for individuals who cannot fight a disease and produce their own antibodies.
In most cases, this type of immunity lasts from a few weeks to several months.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What specific type of acquired immunity do medical vaccines provide when introduced into a healthy human body?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the terms active vs. passive and natural vs. artificial**
* **Active**: The body is exposed to antigens and produces its own antibodies.
* **Passive**: The body receives ready-made antibodies.
* **Natural**: Acquired through normal, biological processes (e.g., catching a cold, maternal milk).
* **Artificial**: Acquired through medical intervention (e.g., vaccination, serum injection).

**Step 2: Apply to vaccines**
A vaccine introduces dead/weakened antigens to stimulate the body to make its own antibodies. Since it is a medical intervention, it is **artificially acquired active immunity**.

**Final Result:**
**Artificially acquired active immunity**.

**Step 1:** Define the types of immunity.
- Active: Body produces its own antibodies.
- Passive: Antibodies are given from another source.

glossary.meaning: Immunity is a term that describes the state of having sufficient defences to avoid infection, disease or other unwanted invasion.
Immunity in which the body makes its own antibodies, after an infection or a vaccine; it is long-lasting.
Immunity from ready-made antibodies received from outside (from the mother or by injection); it is immediate but short-lived.

tips.text: Immunity is the ability of the body to resist infection from exposure to a micro-organism or parasite.

Before any foreign particle establishes itself inside the body of an animal, it has to bypass the physical components of the immune system, such as the skin and mucus, and resist chemical defences (tears, mucus secretions and saliva).
Once the foreign particle gets through the physical barriers, the advanced components of the immune system become active and generate specific antibodies.
Antibodies are proteins produced by white blood cells to specifically fight foreign substances known as antigens.
Antigens are macromolecules that induce certain responses in the immune system.

Immunity is the ability of the body to resist an infectious disease. These can be broadly classified as specific or non-specific components. This type of immunity is called innate (inborn or natural) immunity.

The other components of the immune system, adapt themselves to each new disease encountered and are able to generate a specific type of immunity for a specific pathogen or antigen during the lifetime of an individual.
The components of the immune system are grouped in a type of immunity called acquired immunity.

Inborn immunity refers to a phenomenon in which genetic characteristics common to a particular kind of organism or species provide defences against certain pathogens. Such individuals or species are said to have natural immunity.
For example the immunity of the body against many animal diseases (such as hog cholera, cattle plague, and distemper) and the natural immunity of some individuals to tuberculosis.

questions.q: The trachea and bronchi are lined with a mucous membrane that contains sticky mucus and fine, beating cilia. Which statement correctly describes what happens to bacteria that become trapped in this mucus?

options.A: They are swept downwards by the cilia into the lungs, where they are engulfed by phagocytes in the alveoli.
options.B: They are swept upwards by the cilia to the pharynx, swallowed, and destroyed by the acidic gastric juice in the stomach.
options.C: They are killed exactly where they are trapped by keratin secreted by the ciliated epithelial cells.
options.D: They are dissolved by the fatty acids present in the mucus and then absorbed into the blood.

questions.answer: B
why: **Identify the defence structure.** The trachea and bronchi are lined by the mucociliary escalator, which is part of the non-specific first line of defence and consists of sticky mucus plus fine, beating cilia.
**Trapping of the microbes.** Inhaled bacteria, dust and spores stick to the mucus secreted by the mucous membrane of the air passages.
**Direction of the ciliary beat.** The cilia beat rhythmically and sweep the microbe-laden mucus upwards towards the pharynx; they do not beat downwards into the lungs.
**Chemical destruction in the stomach.** The mucus is swallowed, and the trapped microbes are instantly digested by the highly acidic gastric juice ($$\text{HCl}$$, pH $$1.5$$).

**Test the distractors.** Keratin is a protein of the cornified skin layer, not a secretion of ciliated cells, so C is wrong; fatty acids occur in sweat and sebum on the skin, not in airway mucus, so D is wrong; and because the cilia beat upwards, A is wrong. Only B matches the mucociliary escalator.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A child in Asmara inhales dust carrying bacteria. The bacteria are trapped in the sticky mucus of the air passages. In which organ are these trapped microorganisms finally destroyed by hydrochloric acid?
questions.answer: B. The stomach
why: **Trapping in the airways.** The nasal passages, trachea and bronchi are lined with sticky mucus that traps inhaled bacteria and dust.
**Upward transport.** The cilia beat rhythmically and sweep the dust-laden mucus upwards to the pharynx.
**Swallowing and acid digestion.** The mucus is swallowed into the stomach, where gastric juice ($$\text{HCl}$$, pH $$1.5$$) instantly digests the microorganisms.

**Reject the other options.** The alveoli are below the trachea and the cilia beat upwards, so A is wrong; the lymph nodes and bone marrow are sites where antibodies are manufactured, not sites of acid destruction, so C and D are wrong.

questions.q: Explain the role of the cilia that line the trachea, and state what would happen to the trapped dust and bacteria if these cilia stopped beating.
questions.answer: The cilia beat rhythmically and sweep the sticky mucus, together with the dust and bacteria trapped in it, upwards to the pharynx so that it can be swallowed and destroyed by gastric acid. If the cilia stopped beating, the mucus would no longer be swept upwards: it would accumulate in the air passages and the trapped microorganisms could remain in the respiratory tract and cause infection.
why: **Describe the lining.** The trachea is lined with a mucous membrane that contains goblet cells secreting sticky mucus and ciliated epithelial cells.
**State the normal role of cilia.** The cilia beat rhythmically and move the mucus with its trapped microbes upwards to the pharynx, where it is swallowed and destroyed by gastric acid.

**Predict the consequence of ciliary failure.** Without the ciliary beat the mucus is not transported, so it accumulates and the trapped bacteria and dust stay in the respiratory tract, raising the risk of infection.

questions.q:
A baby girl is born in a health centre in Asmara. Before birth she received maternal antibodies across the placenta, and after birth she received more through colostrum. This natural passive immunity protects her for the first $$6$$ months of life. Assume that $$1$$ month $$= 30$$ days.
(a) For how many days does the maternal antibody protection last?
(b) At the age of $$5$$ months she is given the measles vaccine. Her own B-lymphocytes need $$10$$ days to produce enough antibodies and memory cells. Is there any period during which she is completely unprotected? Show your reasoning.
(c) Name the type of acquired immunity she has once her own antibodies have been produced, and state whether memory cells are present.
questions.answer: (a) $$180$$ days. (b) No gap: her own antibodies appear on day $$160$$ while maternal protection lasts until day $$180$$, giving an overlap of $$20$$ days. (c) Artificial active immunity, with memory cells present.
why: **Classify the immunity from the mother.** Antibodies crossing the placenta and passing in colostrum are ready-made antibodies produced by the mother, so the baby has natural passive immunity; her own cells made none of these antibodies.
**Calculate the duration of maternal protection.** The protection lasts $$6$$ months, and $$1$$ month $$= 30$$ days, so the duration is $$6 \times 30 = 180$$ days.
**Find the day the vaccine is given.** At $$5$$ months of age she is $$5 \times 30 = 150$$ days old when the vaccine is given.
**Find when her own antibodies appear.** Her B-lymphocytes need $$10$$ days after vaccination, so her own protective antibodies appear on day $$150 + 10 = 160$$.

**Check for a gap in protection.** Maternal antibodies protect her until day $$180$$, and her own antibodies begin on day $$160$$. Since $$160 < 180$$, there is no unprotected period; the two protections overlap for $$180 - 160 = 20$$ days.

**Classify the vaccine-induced immunity.** The vaccine supplies antigens that stimulate the girl's own B-lymphocytes to make antibodies, so she develops artificial active immunity, and memory B-cells are formed.
**State the conclusions.** (a) $$180$$ days of maternal protection; (b) no gap, with a $$20$$-day overlap; (c) artificial active immunity, and memory cells are present.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A newborn boy in Keren receives maternal antibodies that give him natural passive immunity for the first $$6$$ months of life. Assume that $$1$$ month $$= 30$$ days. He is given the BCG vaccine at the age of $$4$$ months, and his body needs $$14$$ days to build up protective antibody levels.
(a) How many days does the maternal protection last?
(b) Is there any period during which he is completely unprotected? Show your reasoning and state the number of overlapping days.
questions.answer: (a) $$180$$ days. (b) No gap: his own antibodies appear on day $$134$$ and maternal protection continues until day $$180$$, so there are $$46$$ days of overlap.
why: **Duration of maternal protection.** $$6$$ months at $$30$$ days each gives $$6 \times 30 = 180$$ days of natural passive immunity.
**Day of vaccination.** At $$4$$ months of age the boy is $$4 \times 30 = 120$$ days old.
**Day his own antibodies appear.** His body needs $$14$$ days after vaccination, so his own antibodies appear on day $$120 + 14 = 134$$.
**Compare the two dates.** Since day $$134$$ is earlier than day $$180$$, the boy is never unprotected; the protections overlap for $$180 - 134 = 46$$ days.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A man in Massawa is injected with anti-tetanus serum after a deep wound, and at the same time he begins a course of tetanus vaccine. The injected serum provides ready-made antibodies that protect him for $$21$$ days, while his own B-lymphocytes need $$10$$ days to produce protective antibodies.
(a) Name the type of immunity given by the serum and the type that the vaccine will produce.
(b) Is there any period during which he is unprotected? Show your reasoning.
(c) For how many days do the injected antibodies and his own antibodies overlap?
questions.answer: (a) The serum gives artificial passive immunity; the vaccine produces artificial active immunity. (b) No gap: his own antibodies appear on day $$10$$ while the injected antibodies last until day $$21$$. (c) $$21 - 10 = 11$$ days of overlap.
why: **Classify the serum injection.** Ready-made antibodies produced by another human or animal and injected into the patient give artificial passive immunity, which acts immediately but forms no memory cells.
**Classify the vaccination course.** The vaccine supplies antigens that stimulate the patient's own B-lymphocytes, so it produces artificial active immunity with memory cells.
**Compare the two time courses.** The injected antibodies protect from day $$0$$ to day $$21$$, and his own antibodies begin on day $$10$$.
**Decide whether a gap exists.** Because day $$10$$ comes before day $$21$$, protection is continuous; the overlap is $$21 - 10 = 11$$ days.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A boy in Massawa is bitten by a stray dog suspected of carrying rabies. The doctor immediately injects him with anti-rabies serum and also begins a course of rabies vaccine. Using the types of acquired immunity:
(a) Name the type of acquired immunity provided by the serum injection.
(b) Name the type of acquired immunity that the vaccine course will produce.
(c) Explain why the serum is given immediately but the vaccine cannot protect the boy during the first few days.
(d) State which of the two provides immunological memory.
questions.answer: (a) Artificial passive immunity. (b) Artificial active immunity. (c) The serum already contains ready-made antibodies that bind and neutralise the rabies virus immediately, whereas active immunity takes several days because the boy's own B-lymphocytes must first produce the antibodies. (d) Only the vaccine course, that is artificial active immunity, provides memory cells.
why: **Classify the serum injection.** The serum contains ready-made antibodies produced by another immune human or animal, so it gives artificial passive immunity.
**Classify the vaccine course.** The vaccine contains dead, weakened or fragmented pathogens (antigens) that stimulate the boy's own B-lymphocytes, so it produces artificial active immunity.

**Compare the speeds of protection.** Passive immunity is immediate because the injected antibodies can bind and neutralise the rabies virus at once; active immunity is slow because the body must first detect the antigen and its B-lymphocytes must divide, differentiate into plasma cells and synthesise new antibodies, which takes several days.

**Apply this to the emergency.** Rabies is highly dangerous, so the boy cannot wait several days for his own active response; the ready-made serum neutralises the virus immediately while the vaccine builds long-term protection in the background.

**Decide where memory comes from.** Only the vaccine (artificial active immunity) stimulates the boy's own cells, so only it forms memory B-cells; the injected serum provides no immunological memory and its antibodies are eventually broken down.

questions.q:
A girl in Keren becomes ill with mumps, recovers fully, and is never infected again.
(a) Which type of acquired immunity does she now have?
(b) Would she still need a mumps vaccine later? Explain your answer using the idea of memory cells.
questions.answer: (a) Natural active immunity. (b) No: she already has memory B-cells from the natural infection, and these recognise the mumps pathogen instantly on a second exposure and produce antibodies rapidly, so vaccination is unnecessary.
why: **Identify how the immunity was acquired.** She caught mumps naturally and her own immune system fought the infection, so the immunity is natural active immunity.
**Explain the lasting protection.** During the natural infection her B-lymphocytes produced antibodies and left long-lived memory cells, so protection is long-lasting.
**Answer the vaccine question.** Because memory cells respond immediately if the same pathogen returns, re-infection is prevented and an additional vaccine is not needed.

questions.q:
A newborn baby in Nakfa is fed colostrum, the first breast milk, which is rich in maternal antibodies.
(a) Which type of acquired immunity does the baby receive?
(b) Why does this protection last only about the first $$6$$ months and not a lifetime?
(c) Does the baby form memory cells against the pathogens covered by these antibodies? Explain.
questions.answer: (a) Natural passive immunity. (b) The antibodies are ready-made and were not produced by the baby's own cells, so they are gradually broken down and the protection lasts only a few months (about $$6$$ months in this case). (c) No: because the baby's own B-lymphocytes were never stimulated, no memory cells are formed.
why: **Classify the transferred antibodies.** Antibodies passed from mother to offspring through the placenta or through colostrum give natural passive immunity.

**Explain the short duration.** The baby did not manufacture these antibodies, so they are eventually broken down and the protection lasts only a short time, protecting the infant for about the first $$6$$ months of life.
**Explain the lack of memory.** Since the baby's own B-lymphocytes were not stimulated by the antigens, no memory cells are produced.

questions.q:
During a measles outbreak in a district near Nakfa, health workers study $$4000$$ children. $$3200$$ of the children had previously received the measles vaccine and $$800$$ had never been vaccinated. During the outbreak, $$8\%$$ of the unvaccinated children and $$0.25\%$$ of the vaccinated children contracted measles.
(a) Calculate the number of children who contracted measles in each group.
(b) Calculate the total number of measles cases among the $$4000$$ children.
(c) What percentage of all the measles cases came from the unvaccinated group? Give your answer to one decimal place.
(d) State the type of acquired immunity that the vaccinated children were expected to have, and explain, in terms of memory cells, why so few of them became ill.
questions.answer: (a) $$64$$ unvaccinated children and $$8$$ vaccinated children. (b) $$72$$ measles cases in total. (c) $$88.9\%$$ of the cases came from the unvaccinated group. (d) The vaccinated children were expected to have artificial active immunity; the vaccine antigens made their B-lymphocytes form memory cells, which recognise the measles pathogen quickly on re-exposure and produce antibodies before the disease develops.
why: **List the group sizes.** There are $$800$$ unvaccinated children and $$3200$$ vaccinated children, giving a total of $$4000$$ children studied.
**Cases among the unvaccinated children.** $$8\%$$ of $$800$$ means $$800 \times \frac{8}{100} = 64$$ children contracted measles.
**Cases among the vaccinated children.** $$0.25\%$$ of $$3200$$ means $$3200 \times \frac{0.25}{100} = 3200 \times 0.0025 = 8$$ children contracted measles.
**Total cases in the district.** Adding the two groups gives $$64 + 8 = 72$$ measles cases in total.
**Percentage of cases from the unvaccinated group.** The unvaccinated group contributed $$64$$ of the $$72$$ cases, so the percentage is $$\frac{64}{72} \times 100 = 88.888... \approx 88.9\%$$.

**Explain the difference using immunity.** The vaccinated children were expected to have artificial active immunity: the vaccine antigens stimulated their B-lymphocytes to produce antibodies and memory cells, so on re-exposure to measles the memory cells recognised the pathogen at once and produced antibodies rapidly, preventing the disease from developing.
**State the final answers.** (a) $$64$$ unvaccinated and $$8$$ vaccinated children; (b) $$72$$ cases; (c) $$88.9\%$$; (d) artificial active immunity supported by memory cells.

questions.q:
An oral polio immunization campaign in Asmara covers $$5000$$ children: $$4500$$ children receive the vaccine and $$500$$ remain unvaccinated. In a later outbreak, $$6\%$$ of the unvaccinated children and $$0.2\%$$ of the vaccinated children are infected.
(a) Calculate the number of infected children in each group.
(b) Calculate the total number of infections.
(c) What percentage of all the infections came from the vaccinated group? Give your answer to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) $$30$$ unvaccinated children and $$9$$ vaccinated children. (b) $$39$$ infections in total. (c) $$\frac{9}{39} \times 100 = 23.1\%$$ came from the vaccinated group.
why: **List the group sizes.** There are $$500$$ unvaccinated children and $$4500$$ vaccinated children, giving $$5000$$ children in total.
**Infections among the unvaccinated children.** $$6\%$$ of $$500$$ equals $$500 \times \frac{6}{100} = 30$$ infected children.
**Infections among the vaccinated children.** $$0.2\%$$ of $$4500$$ equals $$4500 \times \frac{0.2}{100} = 4500 \times 0.002 = 9$$ infected children.
**Total infections.** $$30 + 9 = 39$$ infections in total.
**Percentage from the vaccinated group.** The vaccinated group contributed $$9$$ of the $$39$$ infections, so the percentage is $$\frac{9}{39} \times 100 = 23.076... \approx 23.1\%$$.

questions.q:
A health centre in Keren reports that of $$2500$$ children who received the measles vaccine, $$0.4\%$$ later contracted measles, while of the $$500$$ children who were not vaccinated, $$15\%$$ contracted measles.
(a) Calculate the number of cases in each group.
(b) Calculate the total number of cases.
(c) How many times greater was the infection rate among the unvaccinated children than among the vaccinated children?
questions.answer: (a) $$10$$ vaccinated children and $$75$$ unvaccinated children contracted measles. (b) $$85$$ cases in total. (c) The infection rate was $$\frac{15}{0.4} = 37.5$$ times greater among the unvaccinated children.
why: **Cases among the vaccinated children.** $$0.4\%$$ of $$2500$$ equals $$2500 \times \frac{0.4}{100} = 2500 \times 0.004 = 10$$ children.
**Cases among the unvaccinated children.** $$15\%$$ of $$500$$ equals $$500 \times \frac{15}{100} = 75$$ children.
**Total number of cases.** $$10 + 75 = 85$$ cases in total.
**Compare the two infection rates.** The rate in the unvaccinated group was $$15\%$$ and in the vaccinated group $$0.4\%$$, so the ratio is $$\frac{15}{0.4} = 37.5$$ times greater.

**Relate the rates to immunity.** The vaccinated children had artificial active immunity with memory B-cells, which explains the far lower infection rate; the unvaccinated children depended only on non-specific defences and, if infected, on slow natural active immunity.
